All of this revenue currently comes from the United States.

With inflation readings on deck and energy costs shaped by conflict in the Strait of Hormuz, many investors are reassessing how exposed their portfolios are to price shocks and policy moves. Tidewater (TDW)

Tidewater is a Houston based offshore services company that supplies vessels and marine support to oil, gas, and offshore wind projects, which links it closely to the U.S. Energy Sector Stocks theme as offshore exploration and production activity responds to changing energy prices. Revenue is spread across vessel operations in Europe/Mediterranean at about $365 million, West Africa at about $337 million, the Americas at about $259 million, Asia Pacific at about $190 million, the Middle East at about $183 million, plus around $12 million from other operating revenue. The company has a market cap of about US$4.7b, putting it toward the larger end of the offshore services space covered by this screener.

Rising energy prices and renewed offshore spending put Tidewater in focus because its vessels are essential for getting offshore projects drilled, maintained, and eventually decommissioned. Tight vessel supply, improving margins and recent M&A that expands its Brazil footprint point to a business that could benefit if offshore demand stays firm. At the same time, conflict related fuel and crew costs, reliance on cyclical offshore markets, and higher external funding keep risk on the table. For investors who want direct exposure to offshore activity rather than just oil producers, Tidewater offers a focused way into that theme without the whole story being obvious at first glance.

Cactus (WHD)

Cactus gives you direct exposure to onshore drilling and production activity because its engineered wellheads and pressure control gear are installed on unconventional oil and gas wells when rigs are turning and frac crews are working. Most of its revenue, about US$991 million, comes from the Pressure Control segment, with a further US$375 million from Spoolable Technologies that supplies FlexSteel pipe for gathering and production lines, and a small intersegment elimination. With a market cap around US$5.7b, Cactus is one of the larger pure play U.S. energy services stocks tied to upstream capital spending and field activity.

Investors looking at energy as an inflation hedge may find Cactus interesting because it sells the equipment producers need when they step up drilling and completion work in response to higher oil and gas prices. Its Pressure Control and FlexSteel pipe businesses are built around efficiency and field service support, which can matter when customers are watching both costs and uptime. At the same time, Cactus is wrestling with higher input and labor costs and does not always have unlimited room to lift prices, as management commentary on past inflation pressures makes clear. There is also the question of how much you are paying for this exposure today given a rich P/E and recent insider selling. The key issue for investors is whether Cactus can leverage its growing international footprint and product strengths to support margins in an environment where inflation, interest rates and activity levels continue to shift.

RPC (RES)

RPC is tightly linked to the U.S. Energy Sector Stocks theme because it supplies the pressure pumping, cementing, coiled tubing, wireline, and rental tools that oil and gas producers rely on when they drill, complete, and maintain wells. Most of its roughly US$1.8b in revenue comes from the Technical Services segment at about US$1.7b, with around US$89 million from Support Services rental tools and related services. The company has a market cap of about US$1.4b, which puts RPC in the mid cap bracket of oilfield service providers screened for this theme.

If you want direct exposure to how higher oil and gas prices can influence drilling and completion activity, RPC deserves a close look. The company relies on advanced tools and cleaner pressure pumping fleets to win work in North American shale, while a solid balance sheet and extended credit facility give it room to keep upgrading equipment and returning cash.
